title: This Is The Blackest Material Ever Made
description:
Vantablack absorbs 99.965% of the light that hits it -- so much that objects coated in it look flat, like a hole cut into reality. Here's how it actually works.

#shorts #sciencefacts #didyouknow

scenes.text: This material absorbs 99.965% of the light that hits it. It's called Vantablack, and it's the blackest substance ever made.
It isn't paint. It's a dense forest of carbon nanotubes, grown straight up, each one about 3,500 times thinner than a human hair.
Light hitting that forest gets trapped, bouncing between nanotube walls over and over, losing energy as heat each time, until almost none escapes.
Objects coated in it stop looking three dimensional at all. A crumpled sheet just reads as a flat black shape, like a hole cut into the image.
It's used on real spacecraft instruments and telescopes, where blocking out stray light lets sensors pick up incredibly faint signals they'd otherwise miss.

In 2016, artist Anish Kapoor secured exclusive rights to use it in art. Other artists were furious -- one, Stuart Semple, responded by making a hot pink paint available to everyone in the world except Kapoor.
Would you actually want something in your house painted in the blackest material ever made?
